name: LMDB
baseline: SQLite (rusqlite 0.38 bundled, default settings, BLOB PRIMARY KEY table)
workload: redb author's comparison harness: 5M bulk-loaded random pairs (24-byte keys, 150-byte values), 1,000 individual sync writes, batch writes, 1M random point reads, 500k random 10-element range scans, multi-threaded random reads, removals, with a 4 GiB cache setting for the engines that take one; LMDB driven through the Rust heed 0.22 binding.
claimed_speedup: Times in ms, lower is better, as printed in the redb README table (ratios derived from page data): random reads 637 vs 4283 for SQLite (6.7x); random range reads 565 vs 8431 (14.9x); random reads with 16 threads 216 vs 23022 (107x) and with 32 threads 125 vs 26536 (212x); individual writes 1598 vs 7040 (4.4x); batch writes 942 vs 2625 (2.8x); bulk load 9232 vs 15341 (1.7x); removals 10435 vs 10323 (parity). Disk use after load is 2.61 GiB for LMDB vs 1.09 GiB for SQLite (LMDB 2.4x larger).
compiler_and_flags: Rust benchmark crate built through cargo bench (bench profile sets debug = true; rustc version and C compiler flags for the bundled LMDB and SQLite are not stated); heed and rusqlite (bundled SQLite) as pinned in crates/redb-bench-compare/Cargo.toml
hardware: Ryzen 9950X3D with Samsung 9100 PRO NVMe (per README)
stars_or_usage: about 3.0k stars on the GitHub mirror; embedded in OpenLDAP and widely bound from other languages
tradeoffs: Single writer at a time (readers never block); copy-on-write B+tree with no compaction or compression, so the file is larger than compacting engines (the same table shows 2.61 GiB uncompacted vs 893 MiB for RocksDB and 1.09 GiB for SQLite); fixed maximum map size must be chosen up front; no SQL layer or secondary indexes; removals and mixed workloads are less favourable (loses removals to RocksDB and fjall in the same table).
caveats: The numbers come from a competing project's (redb) README, not from the LMDB authors, and LMDB is reached through the heed Rust wrapper. SQLite is run with default settings (no WAL and no tuning pragmas visible in the harness source) in a plain BLOB PRIMARY KEY table, so it is not a best-case SQLite. Compiler version and flags are not stated, which keeps the tier at B rather than A. The primary LMDB claim, the Symas/lmdb.tech microbench against SQLite, BerkeleyDB, Kyoto Cabinet and LevelDB, could not be opened (host blocked), so no numbers from it are recorded. A second, weaker data point from Mozilla's kvbench (mykmelez/kvbench, Rust bindings, hardware not stated) shows LMDB opening a database about 8x faster than LevelDB (166.70 us vs 1.3895 ms, derived from page data) but slower on single synchronous puts (about 114 us vs 58 us).

name: DuckDB
baseline: PostgreSQL (ClickBench configuration: apt postgresql, shared_buffers 25% of RAM, parallel workers, no indexes)
workload: ClickBench: 43 analytical queries over the 100-million-row flat web-analytics hits table, single-node c6a.4xlarge, hot runs (best of the second and third run), plus load time and on-disk size.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (ClickBench result JSON files, best hot run per query summed over 43 queries): DuckDB 24.61 s (result dated 2025-02-05) vs PostgreSQL 3675.3 s (result dated 2025-02-26), about 149x less total time; DuckDB is faster on 33 of the 43 queries and PostgreSQL on 10 (Q7, Q18, Q20 to Q27, mostly selective filter or LIMIT queries where PostgreSQL returns in about 2 ms). Load time 372 s vs 961 s (2.6x); data size 23.65 GB vs 124.2 GB (5.3x smaller).
compiler_and_flags: Not applicable: ClickBench installs the released DuckDB CLI binary (install script pulls the latest release) and the PostgreSQL apt package; no compiler flags are involved.
hardware: AWS c6a.4xlarge (16 vCPU, AMD EPYC 7R13 implied by instance type, 32 GiB) with 500 GB gp2 disk, per the ClickBench README
stars_or_usage: about 42k stars; widely embedded (Python, R, Java, WebAssembly clients)
tradeoffs: Embedded single-process column store aimed at analytics, not a replacement for a multi-user OLTP server: row-at-a-time updates, high-concurrency writes and index-driven point lookups are not its strength (PostgreSQL wins the selective LIMIT-style ClickBench queries); data must be loaded into its own storage format for best speed.
caveats: ClickBench is run by a third party (ClickHouse) with public scripts, but the DuckDB installer pulls the latest release rather than a pinned version, the PostgreSQL run is tagged 'no-cold' (lukewarm cold runs) and 'tuned: no', and the pairing of result files from different dates (2025-02-05 and 2025-02-26) is mine. PostgreSQL results dated 2025-03-10 and 2026-09-21 on the same instance show an implausible flat floor of about 258 s per query (sum about 11,880 s), so they look like a harness artifact and were not used. The 149x total-time ratio is dominated by a few very slow PostgreSQL queries (for example Q3 at 237 s and Q10 at 268 s); the geometric mean of per-query ratios is about 24x (my estimate, clamping PostgreSQL's 2 ms timing floor). CPU model is implied by the instance type, not printed on the results page. DuckDB's own benchmark pages (duckdb.org) were not reachable.
found_via: seed-record pass (seed-list mining backfill): listed in the awesome-cpp and awesome-c Database sections as a fast in-process analytical database; evidence found in the ClickBench repository result files for duckdb and postgresql on c6a.4xlarge

name: Infinity
baseline: Elasticsearch 8.13.4 (full-text and dense vector search); Qdrant 1.9.2 also measured
workload: Repo benchmark doc: full-text OR queries on 33M English Wikipedia documents with 16 Python clients, and L2 vector search on SIFT1M (10,000 queries) and GIST1M (1,000 queries), reporting QPS, recall, P95 latency, index build time, memory and disk.
claimed_speedup: Enwiki full-text: 13731 QPS vs 1340 for Elasticsearch (10.2x, derived from page data), P95 latency 1.37 ms vs 14.75 ms (10.8x, derived), index build 1562 s vs 2289 s (1.5x, derived). SIFT1M vector search: 16320 QPS vs 934 for Elasticsearch (17.5x, derived) and 1303 for Qdrant (12.5x, derived); GIST1M: 2200 QPS vs 305 and 339 (7.2x and 6.5x, derived). Recall is 0.973 vs 0.992 (Elasticsearch) and 0.979 (Qdrant) on SIFT1M.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: Elasticsearch, Qdrant and Infinity run from Docker images (ES_JAVA_OPTS=-Xms16384m -Xmx32000m for Elasticsearch); no compile flags for Infinity.
hardware: Intel Core i5-13500H, 16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB disk, OpenSUSE Tumbleweed x86_64
tradeoffs: Single-node AI-native database whose index and engine are specialised for hybrid search; lower recall than Elasticsearch on SIFT1M (0.973 vs 0.992); needs AVX2 on x86_64; time to build the vector index is slower than Qdrant on both datasets (74 s vs 46 s on SIFT1M insert plus build, 463 s vs 366 s on GIST1M); Elasticsearch uses more memory (21.0 GB vs 10.0 GB on Enwiki) but Infinity needs about the same vCPU.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the Infinity authors on a single laptop-class CPU, 16 Python clients may bound the client side. The doc table says Infinity v0.2.0 (about 2024) but the run command uses the infiniflow/infinity:nightly image, so the exact build is not pinned; the README now ships 0.7.x. Elasticsearch is given a 32 GB maximum heap on a 32 GB machine. Lucene itself is not measured separately (Elasticsearch is built on Lucene). Tier A is given because the benchmark driver (python/benchmark/run.py), dataset links, versions and CPU model are public, but compiler and flags are not applicable or stated and the nightly tag drifts; a stricter reading would put it at C. The README headline claims (0.1 ms vector latency, 15K+ QPS; 1 ms and 12K+ QPS full-text) are in the same range as the doc table.

name: LevelDB
workload: Google's July 2011 db_bench-derived suite: 1 million entries with 16-byte keys and 100-byte values (about 50% compressible), sequential and random reads and writes, 4 MB cache, asynchronous writes, plus batch, synchronous, large-value, no-compression and larger-cache variants.
claimed_speedup: Baseline run, ops/sec LevelDB vs SQLite3: sequential reads 4,030,000 vs 383,000 (10.5x, derived from page data); sequential writes 779,000 vs 48,600 (16.0x, derived); random writes 164,000 vs 9,860 (16.6x, derived); batch random writes 221,000 vs 22,000 entries/s (10x, derived). Not faster everywhere: random reads 129,000 vs 134,000 for SQLite3 and 151,000 for Kyoto TreeDB; 100,000-byte values 1,100 vs 1,600 ops/sec sequential writes and 480 vs 1,600 random writes.
compiler_and_flags: Partly stated: LevelDB built with tcmalloc and Snappy (revision 33), assertions disabled; SQLite3 tuned with exclusive locking mode and write-ahead logging; TreeDB built with LZO 2.03 and TSMALL/TLINEAR options. Compiler and optimization level not stated.
hardware: Six-core Intel Xeon X5650 @ 2.67GHz, 12 MB L3, 12 GB DDR3-1333, SATA 7200 RPM disks, ext3 and ext4 machines
stars_or_usage: about 39.5k stars; used by Chromium (IndexedDB) and many bindings
tradeoffs: LSM tree with ordered keys, no transactions (WriteBatch only), single process access, compaction pauses and write amplification (large values written twice, 1,100 vs 1,600 SQLite ops/sec at 100 KB); only a single process may open a database at a time; no SQL, relational model or indexes and no client-server layer (per its README Limitations).
caveats: Numbers are from 2011 (LevelDB revision 39, SQLite 3.7.6.3) with first-party benchmark code (benchmarks/db_bench.cc, db_bench_sqlite3.cc, db_bench_tree_db.cc in the repo, all present); compiler and flags are not stated, so the tier is C. The file's synchronous-write section is on ext3 and the doc itself says ext4 drops LevelDB to about 31 sync writes per second. The suggested baselines (std::map, RocksDB) are not in the benchmark. Random reads, and large values, are cases where it does not beat the baselines in this same table; Mozilla's kvbench (mykmelez/kvbench, Rust bindings) found LMDB about 8x faster than LevelDB at opening a database.
